etymology: From Old French face, from Latin facies, form or appearance. The Hebrew pānīm is grammatically plural — faces — and is the ordinary word for presence: to be before someone is in Hebrew to be at his faces. This is why the same word carries the shewbread (the bread of the faces), the phrase face to face, and the whole vocabulary of God's presence, favour, and displeasure. The Greek prosōpon is literally that which is toward the eye, and was also the word for an actor's mask — whence the New Testament's idiom for respecting persons is literally receiving faces.
biblical_def: The face in Scripture is presence and disposition together, and the whole of religion can be told in terms of it. The Aaronic blessing asks for the shining face: “The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee” (Num 6:25) — light on the face being favour, as a hidden face is displeasure, and the psalms cry repeatedly, hide not thy face from me. The believer's answering duty is to seek it, and David records the exchange as a summons and a reply: “When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek” (Psa 27:8). Yet there is a limit fixed in this life which no earnestness overcomes: “Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live” (Exo 33:20) — said to Moses, of all men, who spoke with God as a man speaketh unto his friend and who was nevertheless put in a clift of the rock and covered with God's hand while the glory passed by. The gospel's answer to that limit is the heart of the doctrine: God “hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2Co 4:6). The glory that could not be looked at on Sinai is now looked at safely, because it is in a human face. And the promise closes the circle: they shall see his face, and his name shall be in their foreheads.
webster_summary: The countenance, and in Hebrew idiom the presence and disposition of a person; in Scripture the shining face of divine favour, the hidden face of displeasure, the face no man may see and live, and the face of Jesus Christ in which the glory of God is safely beheld.
webster_full: FACE, n. 1. In a general sense, the surface of a thing, or the side which presents itself to the view of the spectator.
2. The forepart of the head of a man, including the forehead, nose, mouth, cheeks and chin.
3. Countenance; cast of features; look; air of the countenance. And in Scripture, the presence of a person; the Hebrew word for face signifying also before or in the presence of.
4. Favor or displeasure, as expressed by the countenance. The LORD make his face shine upon thee. Num. 6. Hide not thy face from me. Psalm 27. Thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled. Psalm 30.
5. To accept, or to respect persons; in the Hebrew and Greek idiom, to receive or lift up the face; a thing forbidden to judges. Levit. 19; James 2.
scriptures: Numbers 6:25
The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee:
Psalm 27:8
When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.
Exodus 33:20
And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.
2 Corinthians 4:6
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: The unseeable face of God is either denied, by a mysticism that promises direct unmediated vision now, or emptied, by a theology that makes God so hidden that Christ's face tells us nothing certain about Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The mystical error promises what Exo 33:20 forbids: an immediate sight of the divine essence available in this life to the sufficiently advanced. Scripture is consistent against it — no man hath seen God at any time; whom no man hath seen, nor can see. What God grants instead is better suited to creatures and is not a lesser thing: the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him. The theophanies of the Old Testament, including the face-to-face speech granted to Moses, are accommodations in which God shews as much as flesh can bear, and they all point forward. To seek an unmediated vision is to seek past the Mediator, and it consistently produces either presumption or despair.

The opposite failure makes God so remote that His self-disclosure in Christ is treated as suggestive rather than decisive — as though behind the face of Jesus there might be a different God, sterner or laxer, whose real disposition is unknown. The New Testament closes that door. He is the image of the invisible God, the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person; he that hath seen me hath seen the Father. This is of enormous pastoral consequence for anyone who fears that God's settled disposition toward him is other than what Christ has shewn. There is no undisclosed God behind the disclosed one. The face that was set like a flint to go to Jerusalem, that was spit upon and marred more than any man's, is the face in which the glory of God is given us to see.
roots_summary: Hebrew pānīm is plural in form and means face, presence, or before; it underlies the shewbread (bread of the faces) and the whole idiom of seeking or hiding the face. Greek prosōpon means face, countenance, or person, and gives the phrase rendered respect of persons.
roots_lines: Hebrew pānīm (H6440) — face, faces, presence, before; over 2,100 occurrences, the commonest way of saying in the presence of.
Hebrew lechem happānīm — the bread of the faces, rendered shewbread; bread set perpetually before the presence of the LORD.
Hebrew pānīm 'el pānīm — face to face; used of the LORD speaking with Moses (Exo 33:11) and of Jacob at Peniel, I have seen God face to face (Gen 32:30).
Greek prosōpon (G4383) — face, countenance, presence, person; used in 2Co 4:6 and in 1Co 13:12, then face to face.
Greek prosōpolepsia (G4382) — respect of persons, literally receiving of faces; a thing forbidden in judgment and denied of God (Rom 2:11).
usage: Of favour and its withdrawal: the LORD make his face shine upon thee (Num 6:25); hide not thy face from thy servant (Psa 69:17).
Of seeking God: seek ye my face (Psa 27:8); if my people shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face (2Ch 7:14).
Of the limit and its answer in Christ: thou canst not see my face (Exo 33:20); the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2Co 4:6); they shall see his face (Rev 22:4).

etymology: From Old Norse gift, related to Old English giefu and to the verb give; the root sense is simply a giving. The Greek is more precise than the English and the New Testament exploits it: dōron is a present, dōrea a free gift with the emphasis on its gratuity, and charisma a gift of grace — formed directly on charis, grace, so that a charisma is grace taking a particular shape in a particular person.
biblical_def: The word gift carries the doctrine of grace in miniature, because a gift by definition is not wages. Paul builds the whole contrast on it: “the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom 6:23) — one side of the sentence is earned and paid, the other is given, and the two halves cannot be blended. He states it again with every avenue of self-congratulation closed: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and adds, not of works, lest any man should boast. The Lord Jesus uses the word of Himself and of the Spirit at the well — “If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink” (Joh 4:10) — where the woman's ignorance, not her unworthiness, is what stands between her and living water. James then extends the principle to the whole of providence: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (Jas 1:17). Nothing good comes from any other quarter, and the Giver does not change — which is the ground of assurance, since a gift is only as secure as the constancy of the one who gave it. Scripture also speaks of gifts distributed for service, dividing to every man severally as the Spirit will, and of the unspeakable gift for which no name is adequate.
webster_summary: A thing freely bestowed; in Scripture the governing word for salvation as opposed to wages, the term for Christ and the Spirit given to sinners, the description of every good thing in providence as descending from an unchanging Father, and the name of graces distributed for service.
webster_full: GIFT, n. 1. A present; any thing given or bestowed; any thing the property of which is voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation.
2. The act of giving or conferring. The gift of God is eternal life. Rom. 6.
3. A bribe; something given to corrupt the judgment. A gift doth blind the eyes of the wise. Deut. 16. In this sense the law strictly forbids the receiving of gifts by judges.
4. A faculty or power bestowed; as the gifts of the Spirit, distributed to every man severally as he will. 1 Cor. 12.
5. In law, a gift is distinguished from a sale or exchange in that no price or consideration passes; whence the theological use, that salvation given for a price would not be a gift at all.
scriptures: Romans 6:23
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Ephesians 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
John 4:10
Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
James 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
corruption_summary: The freeness of the gift is undone in two directions: by systems that attach a price or a condition of merit to it, and by a cheap-grace preaching that keeps the word gift while dropping the repentance and faith by which it is actually received.
corruption_paragraphs: Any scheme in which salvation is partly earned has ceased to describe a gift, whatever it calls itself. Rome's treasury of merit, its indulgences, and its insistence that justification is by an infused righteousness cooperated with, all attach a price; and the Reformation's recovery was precisely at this point, that we are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. But the same error grows readily on Protestant soil in subtler forms — where assurance is made to rest on the quality of one's repentance, the intensity of one's experience, or the consistency of one's service, the gift has quietly become a wage again. Isaiah's invitation is the standing rebuke: come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

The opposite abuse keeps the vocabulary of gift and empties it of everything else. If salvation is free, it is argued, then nothing follows from it, and repentance, obedience, and perseverance become optional extras. Scripture never separates what it distinguishes. The gift is received by faith, and the faith that receives it is itself God's gift and is never alone in the person justified; Eph 2:8-9 is immediately followed by Eph 2:10, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Works are excluded from the ground of salvation and required as its fruit. A gift that leaves the recipient wholly unchanged was not this gift.
roots_summary: Hebrew mattānâh is a present or offering; minchâh is a tribute or meat offering. Greek distinguishes dōron (a present), dōrea (a free gift), and charisma (a gift of grace), all three used deliberately in the epistles.
roots_lines: Hebrew mattānâh (H4979) — a gift, a present; used of gifts among men and of the Levites given as a gift for the service of the tabernacle (Num 18:6).
Hebrew minchâh (H4503) — a gift, tribute, or meat offering; the word for Cain's and Abel's offerings in Gen 4.
Greek dōrea (G1431) — a free gift, with stress on its gratuity; used of the gift of the Holy Ghost (Act 2:38) and of the unspeakable gift (2Co 9:15).
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; formed on charis, grace. Used of eternal life (Rom 6:23) and of gifts for service (1Co 12:4).
Greek opsonion (G3800) — a soldier's rations or wages; the word set against charisma in Rom 6:23 — sin pays, God gives.
usage: Of salvation as opposed to wages: the gift of God is eternal life (Rom 6:23); it is the gift of God, not of works (Eph 2:8-9).
Of Christ and the Spirit given: the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee (Joh 4:10); ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost (Act 2:38).
Of providence and of service: every good gift is from above (Jas 1:17); having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us (Rom 12:6).

etymology: From Old French pris, from Latin pretium, value or reward — the same root that gives precious, praise, and appreciate. The Greek timē is the same word rendered honour elsewhere, since to price a thing and to honour it are one act in the ancient vocabulary: what a man values he pays for. The redemption texts exploit this exactly, since the price paid for the church is what declares her worth to the One who paid it.
biblical_def: Price in Scripture is the language of redemption, and the doctrine turns on a single fact: a price was actually paid. “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's” (1Co 6:20) — and the conclusion drawn is ownership, not merely gratitude. A purchased man is not his own. The price is named elsewhere as the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, and set expressly against corruptible things like silver and gold. The Lord's parable puts the transaction from the buyer's side: the merchant, “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Mat 13:46) — a total expenditure for a single object, gladly made. Scripture also uses price to name what God values in a person, and His valuations are startling: “the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4), an estimate no market would confirm. And the gospel invitation is put in the language of price precisely to exclude it: “come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1). The two truths stand together without strain. The salvation is free to the receiver because it was costly to the Giver; what is priceless to us was not priceless to Him.
webster_summary: The value or sum paid for a thing; in Scripture the vocabulary of redemption — the church bought with a price and therefore not her own — the merchant's total expenditure for the pearl, God's estimate of a meek and quiet spirit, and the free invitation to buy without money.
webster_full: PRICE, n. 1. The sum or amount of money at which a thing is valued, or the value which a seller sets on his goods in market.
2. Value; estimation; excellence; worth. The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. 1 Pet. 3.
3. Reward; recompense. The price of blood; the thirty pieces of silver, which the chief priests would not put into the treasury. Matt. 27.
4. In Scripture, the ransom or purchase money of redemption. Ye are bought with a price. 1 Cor. 6. Not with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ. 1 Pet. 1.
5. Without price; freely; without cost to the receiver. Buy wine and milk without money and without price. Isa. 55.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 6:20
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
Matthew 13:46
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
1 Peter 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Isaiah 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
corruption_summary: The ransom language is dismissed as a crude commercial metaphor unworthy of God, and with it goes penal substitution — leaving an atonement that demonstrates love without accomplishing anything.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern objections to the price language usually take one of two forms. The first asks to whom the ransom was paid, and, finding no satisfactory answer in a payment to Satan, concludes that the whole category is confused. The Reformed answer has never been that the price was paid to the devil, who has no just claim to satisfy; it was paid to God, whose law and justice were the real obstacle. The second objection calls the transaction immoral — the punishment of an innocent for the guilty. This misses the union that Scripture everywhere assumes: Christ is not a random substitute but the covenant head of His people, who freely laid down His life, no man taking it from Him. Where the price is denied, what remains is usually the moral influence theory, in which the cross demonstrates God's love but secures nothing; and a demonstration of love that saves no one is not obviously loving.

There is a second corruption on the practical side, and Paul draws it out himself. Because ye are bought with a price, he says, therefore glorify God in your body — and the argument is aimed at fornication. The purchased man does not own the thing he is misusing. Our age holds the exactly contrary axiom, that a person's body is his own and that this settles every question about what may be done with it or to it. Scripture's answer is not that the body is unimportant but that it is bought, a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Ghost. That is a higher valuation of the body than autonomy ever gives it, and it is the reason the sixth and seventh commandments bind.
roots_summary: Hebrew m'chīr is a price or hire. Greek timē means both price and honour; agorazō is to buy in the market, and exagorazō to buy out — the verb used of redeeming from the curse of the law.
roots_lines: Hebrew m'chīr (H4242) — price, hire, wages; used in 2Sa 24:24, neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing.
Hebrew gā'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; the Old Testament's legal machinery of redemption by a near relative, fulfilled in Christ.
Greek timē (G5092) — price, value, honour; the word in 1Co 6:20 and in Act 5:2, of the price of Ananias's land.
Greek agorazō (G59) — to buy in the market place; used in Rev 5:9, thou hast redeemed us to God by thy blood.
Greek exagorazō (G1805) — to buy out, to redeem from; used in Gal 3:13, Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.
usage: Of redemption and its consequence: ye are bought with a price (1Co 6:20); not with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ (1Pe 1:18-19).
Of total expenditure for one object: one pearl of great price (Mat 13:46); the treasure hid in a field, for joy whereof he selleth all that he hath (Mat 13:44).
Of God's valuation and of free invitation: of great price in the sight of God (1Pe 3:4); buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isa 55:1).

pos: adj. and n. (rendering Hebrew 'ānī, dal, 'ebyōn, and Greek ptōchos, penēs)
etymology: From Old French povre, from Latin pauper. The biblical languages are far more discriminating than the English. Hebrew dal is the low or thin, the weak of estate; 'ānī is the afflicted or bowed down; 'ebyōn is the needy who must beg. Greek distinguishes penēs, the working man who is poor but supports himself, from ptōchos, the destitute beggar who has nothing at all — and it is ptōchos, the harder word, that stands in the first beatitude.
biblical_def: Scripture treats poverty with a seriousness that neither romanticises nor despises it. God is emphatically the poor man's defender: “This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles” (Psa 34:6), and the law is thick with provisions on his behalf — gleanings left, the pledge returned before sundown, no interest charged, judgment not wrested. Charity toward him is framed as a transaction with God Himself: “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again” (Pro 19:17), which makes generosity an investment with the safest possible security. The Son's incarnation is described in the same economic terms: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich” (2Co 8:9) — and Paul's purpose in citing it is to move a church to give. Above all, poverty becomes the picture of the only posture in which the kingdom can be received: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3). The word is the beggar's word. To be poor in spirit is not modesty about one's gifts but the bankrupt's empty hand held out — the recognition that one has nothing to bring, which is precisely why the kingdom can be given.
webster_summary: Wholly or largely destitute of means; in Scripture the object of God's particular defence and of laws framed for his protection, the condition Christ voluntarily entered to enrich others, and, in the first beatitude, the beggar's empty-handedness before God to which the kingdom is promised.
webster_full: POOR, a. 1. Wholly destitute of property, or not having the means of comfortable subsistence.
2. In Scripture, the poor are the special charge of the law and the peculiar care of God, who is called the helper of the fatherless and the judge of the widow.
3. Of little worth; trifling; as a poor excuse. Also, in a good sense, humble; contrite; dejected in spirit. To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit. Isa. 66.
4. Poor in spirit; humble; sensible of one's own want and unworthiness; the first character of the citizens of the kingdom. Matt. 5.
5. The Greek distinguishes the laborer who is poor from the beggar who is destitute; the latter word is used in the beatitude, and denotes one who has nothing whatever of his own.
scriptures: Matthew 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
2 Corinthians 8:9
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
Proverbs 19:17
He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
Psalm 34:6
This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.
corruption_summary: Poverty is made either a moral status conferring innocence, or a proof of personal failure, and 2Co 8:9 is pressed into a doctrine of guaranteed material wealth — each reading replacing the biblical account of the poor with a political or commercial one.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology makes the poor a class that is righteous by virtue of being poor, and salvation a matter of their political liberation; and the corresponding evangelical error treats poverty as prima facie evidence of sloth or of insufficient faith. Scripture supports neither. It condemns the oppression of the poor in the strongest terms and warns that he who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker; it also says plainly that the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty, and that he who will not work shall not eat. It holds both because it deals with people rather than with classes. Proverbs even warns against partiality toward the poor in judgment as well as toward the mighty — thou shalt not respect the person of the poor — because justice is not improved by being tilted in a sympathetic direction.

The prosperity teaching's use of 2Co 8:9 deserves separate notice, since it reverses the verse's plain purpose. Paul is not promising his readers money; he is asking them for it, and the whole chapter is about a collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem. The riches Christ's poverty purchases are the unsearchable riches of Christ, and the Macedonians whom Paul holds up as the model gave out of deep poverty and much affliction. Christ was in fact poor — born in a borrowed stable, buried in a borrowed tomb, with nowhere to lay His head — and the doctrine drawn from it in Scripture is generosity, not acquisition. Meanwhile the first beatitude keeps the deeper sense in view, since the poverty that must be confessed by rich and poor alike is the poverty of the beggar before God.
roots_summary: Hebrew has a family of terms: dal (low, weak), 'ānī (afflicted, bowed down), 'ebyōn (needy, begging), and rush (in want). Greek separates penēs, the poor labourer, from ptōchos, the destitute beggar — the word of the first beatitude.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ānī (H6041) — afflicted, poor, humble; from a root meaning to be bowed down. Used of the Messiah in Zec 9:9, lowly, and riding upon an ass.
Hebrew dal (H1800) — low, weak, thin, poor; the word in Lev 19:15, thou shalt not respect the person of the poor.
Hebrew 'ebyōn (H34) — needy, one who begs; used in Deu 15:11, the poor shall never cease out of the land.
Greek ptōchos (G4434) — a beggar, one destitute and crouching; the word in Mat 5:3 and in the parable of Lazarus.
Greek penēs (G3993) — a poor man who works for his living; used once, in 2Co 9:9, he hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor.
usage: Of God's defence and the law's provision: this poor man cried, and the LORD heard him (Psa 34:6); thou shalt not glean thy vineyard (Lev 19:10).
Of charity as lending to God: he that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD (Pro 19:17); he that giveth unto the poor shall not lack (Pro 28:27).
Of Christ's poverty and of poverty of spirit: for your sakes he became poor (2Co 8:9); blessed are the poor in spirit (Mat 5:3).

etymology: From Old English frēond, the present participle of frēogan, to love — so that a friend is literally a loving one. The Greek keeps the same tie: philos belongs to the phileō family of affectionate love. The Hebrew 'ōhēb is likewise the participle of 'āhab, to love, and it is that word which gives Abraham his title, the friend — the lover — of God.
biblical_def: Friendship in Scripture is a covenantal bond with duties attached, not a mere congeniality. Proverbs gives its cost and its candour: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother” (Pro 18:24), and elsewhere, faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful — so that a friend is defined partly by his willingness to say what will not be welcome. Its highest human form is David and Jonathan, whose souls were knit together and who made a covenant, Jonathan stripping himself of his robe and giving it to the man who would take his father's throne. Its highest form altogether is divine. Abraham “was called the Friend of God” (Jas 2:23), a title given in the same breath as his justification by faith. And the Lord Jesus grants the name to His disciples with a stated reason: “Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (Joh 15:15). Friendship there is defined by disclosure — a servant is told what to do, a friend is told what is going on. And the measure of it is given two verses earlier: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13), spoken by One who was about to do it, and for those who would shortly forsake Him.
webster_summary: One who loves, and in Scripture one bound by covenant affection with duties of faithfulness and candour; the title given to Abraham, the name Christ grants His disciples on the ground that He has disclosed the Father's mind to them, and a bond measured by the laying down of life.
webster_full: FRIEND, n. 1. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company, and to seek to promote his happiness.
2. One not hostile; as, he is no friend to virtue. Also, a favorer; one propitious.
3. The word is the participle of the old verb to free or to love; a friend is a loving one.

4. In Scripture, a title of Abraham, who was called the friend of God; and of the disciples, whom Christ called friends because he had made known to them all things heard of the Father. James 2; John 15.
5. A term of address, sometimes of gentle reproof. Friend, how camest thou in hither, not having a wedding garment? Matt. 22. Friend, wherefore art thou come? Matt. 26.
scriptures: Proverbs 18:24
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
John 15:13
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
John 15:15
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
James 2:23
And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.
corruption_summary: Friendship with Christ is taken to mean familiarity that levels the difference between the Lord and His servants, while the corresponding warning — that friendship with the world is enmity with God — is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Joh 15:15 has been read as though Christ had resigned His lordship in favour of companionship, and a great deal of contemporary devotional language follows — Jesus as a mate, a supporter, an affirming presence with no authority in the relation. The text will not carry it. He says ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you, in the very sentence, and He had washed their feet a chapter earlier while telling them plainly, ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am. The friendship He grants is not the abolition of the servant relation but its enrichment by disclosure. He still commands; He now also confides. Losing either half ruins it: a Lord who never confides makes a religion of bare duty, and a friend who never commands makes a religion of sentiment.

James, who records Abraham's title as the friend of God, is also the writer who states the sharpest antithesis in the New Testament on the subject: know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God. The two verses come from the same pen and the same understanding of what friendship is — an alliance of affection and interest. One cannot be an ally of two parties at war. This is why Proverbs makes candour essential to friendship and warns that he that walketh with wise men shall be wise, but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Friendship is formative, and the biblical counsel is not to have fewer friends but to know what a friendship is doing to the man in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew rēa' is a companion or neighbour; 'ōhēb, a loving one, gives Abraham his title. Greek philos is a friend in the affectionate sense, from phileō, and philia is the friendship James sets against the love of God.
roots_lines: Hebrew rēa' (H7453) — friend, companion, neighbour; the word in thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Lev 19:18) and in the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6).
Hebrew 'ōhēb (H157, participle) — one loving; used in 2Ch 20:7 and Isa 41:8 of Abraham, my friend, literally my lover.
Greek philos (G5384) — a friend, one dear; used in Joh 15:13-15 and of the friend at midnight (Luk 11:5).
Greek philia (G5373) — friendship; occurring once, in Jas 4:4, the friendship of the world is enmity with God.
Greek hetairos (G2083) — a companion, comrade; the cooler word the Lord uses to Judas in the garden, Friend, wherefore art thou come? (Mat 26:50).
usage: Of human friendship and its duties: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24); faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6); the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David (1Sa 18:1).
Of friendship with God: Abraham was called the Friend of God (Jas 2:23); the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend (Exo 33:11).
Of Christ's friendship and its cost: I have called you friends (Joh 15:15); greater love hath no man than this (Joh 15:13).

etymology: From Latin statutum, that which is set up or established, from statuere, to set — the same root as stand and statue. The Hebrew is even more concrete: chōq comes from chāqaq, to cut, to engrave, to inscribe — a statute is something cut in, carved on stone or tablet, and therefore fixed and not to be revised by the reader. The English and the Hebrew agree in making permanence the point.
biblical_def: The statutes are the engraved, fixed appointments of God for His people, and the Old Testament ordinarily lists them alongside commandments and judgments as one of the branches of the law. Their purpose is stated as mercy rather than mere authority: “And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive” (Deu 6:24) — for our good always, which is the answer to every suspicion that God's law is arbitrary restriction. Their character is likewise commended: “The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes” (Psa 19:8). The believer's proper relation to them is neither grudging compliance nor indifference but delight, expressed in one of the most striking lines of the long psalm: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54) — the law set to music by a man on the road. But Scripture is honest that the statutes cannot of themselves produce obedience in a fallen heart, which is why the new covenant promise is not a better code but a changed man: “And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them” (Eze 36:27). The law remains what it was; the difference lies in the Spirit given, and in a heart of flesh replacing the heart of stone.
webster_summary: An engraved and established appointment of God, listed with the commandments and judgments as a branch of His law; given for the good of His people, right and heart-rejoicing, sung by the pilgrim, and kept only where the Spirit causes a man to walk in them.
webster_full: STATUTE, n. 1. An act of the legislature of a state that extends its binding force to all the citizens or subjects of that state; a positive law.
2. A special law for the government of a corporation or society; the statutes of a university.
3. In Scripture, an ordinance or appointment of God; the Hebrew word signifying that which is engraven or cut in, and thus fixed and permanent. Exod. 12; Levit. 3.
4. Statutes, judgments and commandments; the usual threefold division of the Mosaic law in the books of Moses and in the Psalms.
5. A statute for ever; an ordinance appointed to continue throughout the generations of Israel, as the passover and the day of atonement. Levit. 16.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:24
And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as it is at this day.
Psalm 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
Psalm 119:54
Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage.
Ezekiel 36:27
And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
corruption_summary: God's statutes are treated as an obsolete legal code, so that the whole law is either discarded as bondage or re-imposed indiscriminately — both failing to distinguish the moral law that abides from the ceremonial and civil appointments fulfilled in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomianism reasons that because the believer is not under law but under grace, the statutes have no further claim on him. Paul asks and answers the question directly: do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law. The law cannot justify a sinner — that was never its office — but it remains the revelation of God's character and the rule of gratitude for those He has saved. The Reformed tradition speaks of its three uses: it restrains evil in society, it convicts the sinner and drives him to Christ, and it guides the believer in the way of holiness. Where the third use is lost, sanctification loses its shape, and Christians are left sincere and directionless.

The opposite error takes the whole Mosaic corpus as binding without distinction, and so reimposes dietary laws, festival calendars, and the judicial penalties of Israel's civil polity on the Christian church. Scripture itself makes the distinctions. The ceremonial statutes were shadows of things to come, the body being Christ's; the Lord declared all meats clean; the civil statutes governed a particular nation in a particular land under a covenant that has expired with that polity, though their general equity remains instructive. The moral law, summarised in the ten commandments and by Christ in the two great commandments, binds all men always because it reflects God's unchanging nature. Eze 36:27 remains the hope in every case: the promise is not a lighter law but a Spirit who causes His people to walk in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew chōq and its feminine chuqqâh come from chāqaq, to cut or engrave, and so name a fixed, inscribed decree. They stand alongside mitsvâh (commandment), mishpāt (judgment), and tōrâh (law, instruction).
roots_lines: Hebrew chōq (H2706) — a statute, a decree, an appointed portion; from chāqaq (H2710), to cut in, to engrave, to inscribe.
Hebrew chuqqâh (H2708) — ordinance, statute; the feminine form, used of the passover and the day of atonement as a statute for ever.
Hebrew mishpāt (H4941) — judgment, ordinance, legal decision; the case-law branch, usually paired with statutes.
Hebrew mitsvâh (H4687) — commandment, precept; the direct charge, as in the ten commandments.
Hebrew tōrâh (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; from yārâh, to point or teach — the whole body of divine teaching within which the statutes stand.
usage: Of the law's purpose and character: to do all these statutes…for our good always (Deu 6:24); the statutes of the LORD are right (Psa 19:8).
Of the believer's delight: thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage (Psa 119:54); I will delight myself in thy statutes (Psa 119:16).
Of the new covenant remedy: I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Eze 36:27).

etymology: From Old English clāne, pure, clear, unmixed — originally with a strong sense of bright or unobstructed rather than merely washed. The Greek katharos gives English catharsis and Cathar; the Hebrew tāhōr is the technical term of the Levitical system. In Scripture the word is almost always ritual or moral rather than hygienic: clean and unclean are standings before God, not degrees of dirt.
biblical_def: Cleanness in Scripture is a matter of fitness to approach God, and the Levitical system existed to teach it by a thousand daily distinctions. The priests' charge was “that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean” (Lev 10:10) — given immediately after Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire, so that the command to discriminate is delivered over the bodies of two men who did not. The uncleanness in question is contracted by touching death, by disease, by discharge, by certain foods; almost none of it is sin in itself, and all of it excludes from the sanctuary. The whole apparatus is a standing lesson that God is holy and that access is not casual. David goes past the ritual to what it signified, asking for what no water could give: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me” (Psa 51:10) — and the verb is create, the word used of God making the heavens, because the thing needed is not a washing but a making. The New Testament brings the two together. The Lord Jesus declared all meats clean and located defilement in the heart, and He told the disciples the ground of their cleanness: “Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you” (Joh 15:3). Paul draws the conclusion for the conscience: “Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure” (Tit 1:15).
webster_summary: Free from defilement and therefore fit to approach God; in Scripture a ritual and moral standing rather than a matter of hygiene, taught by the Levitical distinctions, sought by David as a new creation of the heart, and given to the disciples through Christ's word.
webster_full: CLEAN, a. 1. Free from dirt, or other foul matter; as clean water; clean hands.
2. Free from moral impurity; innocent. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Job 14.
3. In the Mosaic law, free from ceremonial defilement, and therefore permitted to approach the sanctuary and to be numbered with the congregation. Levit. 10.
4. Clean beasts; those which under the law might be eaten and offered in sacrifice, being distinguished from the unclean. Levit. 11; Gen. 7.
5. CLEAN, adv. Quite; perfectly; fully; entirely. Is his mercy clean gone for ever? Psalm 77.
scriptures: Leviticus 10:10
And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;
Psalm 51:10
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
John 15:3
Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.
Psalm 24:4
He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.
corruption_summary: Tit 1:15 is quoted as though it abolished all moral discrimination for the believer, and the clean-unclean distinction is dismissed as primitive taboo — when the passage is about the conscience of the observer and the distinction was God's own tutor in holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: “Unto the pure all things are pure” is regularly cited to justify whatever the speaker wishes to justify, as though a pure man could handle anything without harm. Paul's subject is narrower and his target is the opposite error. He is writing against Judaizing teachers at Crete who were imposing fables and commandments of men, forbidding foods and multiplying ceremonial scruples, and his point is that the creature is not defiling — every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused if it be received with thanksgiving. The verse frees the conscience from man-made prohibitions; it says nothing whatever about sin, which the same epistle goes on to name plainly, teaching us that denying ungodliness and worldly lusts we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world.

The other reduction treats Leviticus as arbitrary tribal taboo, embarrassing to modern readers and safely discarded. But the system is coherent and deliberately pedagogical: what makes unclean is overwhelmingly connected with death, disease, and disorder — corpses, leprosy, issues, the mixing of what God made distinct — so that Israel was taught in her body, every day, that death has no place near the living God. And the direction of contagion is worth noticing, because it reverses at the incarnation. Under the law, touching the leper made the clean man unclean; when the Lord Jesus put forth his hand and touched the leper, the leprosy departed. That is the gospel in a gesture, and it is why the abolished ceremonies still repay study rather than dismissal.
roots_summary: Hebrew tāhōr (clean, pure) stands against tāmē' (unclean), the pair governing the Levitical system. Greek katharos is clean or pure, giving katharizō, to cleanse, the verb of the leper's healing and of 1Jo 1:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew tāhōr (H2889) — clean, pure, unmixed; used of clean beasts, of pure gold, and of the clean heart in Psa 51:10.
Hebrew tāmē' (H2931) — unclean, defiled; the opposing term, and the cry the leper was required to make, Unclean, unclean (Lev 13:45).
Hebrew bārā' (H1254) — to create; the verb David chooses in Psa 51:10, used elsewhere only of God, and never of working with existing material.
Greek katharos (G2513) — clean, pure, free from admixture; used in Mat 5:8, the pure in heart, and Joh 15:3, now ye are clean.
Greek katharizō (G2511) — to cleanse, to make clean, to pronounce clean; used of the cleansing of lepers and in 1Jo 1:9, to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
usage: Of the Levitical distinction: put difference between the unclean and the clean (Lev 10:10); of every clean beast thou shalt take to thee by sevens (Gen 7:2).
Of the heart: create in me a clean heart, O God (Psa 51:10); he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart (Psa 24:4).
Of the believer's cleansing and conscience: ye are clean through the word (Joh 15:3); unto the pure all things are pure (Tit 1:15).

etymology: From Old French pur, from Latin purus, clean, unmixed, unadulterated. The core idea is not merely the absence of dirt but the absence of admixture — pure gold is gold with nothing else in it. The Hebrew zāk is used of beaten olive oil and pure frankincense; bar is clear or bright. Greek adds hagnos, pure in the sense of chaste and holy, from the same root as hagios, holy — so that in Greek purity and holiness are relatives.
biblical_def: Purity in Scripture is singleness — the absence of what does not belong — and it is required most stringently in the heart, where mixture is most easily hidden. “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mat 5:8), which sets an impossible standard for the natural man and thereby throws him upon the promise of a created clean heart. Scripture applies the word first to God's own speech: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6) — refined to the point where no dross remains, which is the doctrine of Scripture's purity stated in the vocabulary of metallurgy. It governs the Christian's thinking, since Paul's list of what the mind is to dwell on includes “whatsoever things are pure” (Php 4:8), the command being about the direction of attention rather than merely about the avoidance of what is filthy. And James defines the purity of religion itself in terms that would surprise most people who use the phrase: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27) — two halves, mercy toward the helpless and separation from the world's defilement, and the religion that has one without the other is not the pure article.
webster_summary: Free from admixture; in Scripture singleness of heart before God, the refined and dross-free character of His words, a governing standard for the Christian's thinking, and, in James, a definition of religion itself as mercy to the helpless joined to separation from the world.
webster_full: PURE, a. 1. Separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter; clear; free from mixture; as pure water; pure gold.
2. Free from moral defilement; without spot; not sullied or tarnished. Blessed are the pure in heart. Matt. 5.
3. Genuine; real; true; incorrupt; as pure religion; the pure word of God.
4. Chaste; as a pure virgin. In this sense the Greek employs a distinct word, signifying also holy and sacred.
5. Mere; absolute; that and nothing else; as pure grace, that is, grace with no admixture of merit whatever.
scriptures: Matthew 5:8
Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.
Psalm 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Philippians 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
James 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Purity is reduced to a single department of conduct and then either policed harshly as an outward code or abandoned as repressive, while the biblical thing — singleness of heart toward God — goes unaddressed by both.
corruption_paragraphs: Where purity is treated as an external code, it produces the Pharisee, who makes clean the outside of the cup and platter while within is full of extortion and excess. The Lord's beatitude aims deeper than any code can reach: pure in heart, which no one can inspect and no rule can secure. That is why the beatitudes are not entrance requirements to be achieved but a portrait of the citizens of the kingdom, and why they open with poverty of spirit. A man who begins by admitting he has nothing is in a position to receive a pure heart; a man who begins by producing one has already failed. The reaction against external codes then swings to the opposite error, treating any call to purity as repression — which leaves the heart exactly as divided as it was and adds a theory that the division is health.

James supplies the corrective that both sides need, and it is jarring by design. Asked to define pure religion, he does not name doctrine, though he holds it firmly, nor devotional practice, though he commends it. He names visiting the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and keeping oneself unspotted from the world — active mercy toward those who cannot repay it, joined to a refusal of the world's defilements. The two halves are what each error drops. Religion that is only separation becomes sterile and censorious; religion that is only compassion is absorbed by the world it means to help. Purity is having nothing in it that does not belong — and, just as much, having in it everything that does.
roots_summary: Hebrew tāhōr is ritually and morally clean; zāk is pure and unmixed, used of beaten oil and pure incense; bar is clear. Greek katharos is clean or unmixed, and hagnos is pure in the sense of chaste and sacred, cognate with hagios, holy.
roots_lines: Hebrew tāhōr (H2889) — clean, pure; used of pure gold in the sanctuary furnishings and of the pure heart of Psa 24:4.
Hebrew zāk (H2134) — pure, unmixed; used of pure olive oil beaten for the light (Exo 27:20) and of pure frankincense (Exo 30:34).
Hebrew tsāraph (H6884) — to refine, to smelt, to try as metal; the verb behind purified seven times in Psa 12:6.
Greek katharos (G2513) — clean, pure, free from admixture; the word of the beatitude in Mat 5:8.
Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste, holy; used in Php 4:8 of whatsoever things are pure, and in 1Jo 3:3, he that hath this hope purifieth himself, even as he is pure.
usage: Of the heart before God: blessed are the pure in heart (Mat 5:8); who can say, I have made my heart clean? (Pro 20:9).
Of Scripture and of God's ways: the words of the LORD are pure words (Psa 12:6); every word of God is pure (Pro 30:5).
Of thought and of religion: whatsoever things are pure (Php 4:8); pure religion and undefiled before God (Jas 1:27).

pos: adj. and v. (rendering Hebrew chōl, chālal, and Greek bebēlos)
etymology: From Latin profanus — pro (before, outside) plus fanum (a temple): literally outside the temple, and hence common, unconsecrated, and by extension irreverent. The Hebrew chōl means simply the common as opposed to the holy, and the verb chālal means to bore through, to wound, and so to violate what was set apart. The Greek bebēlos is built the same way as the Latin: bēlos, a threshold — what may be walked on by anyone.
biblical_def: To profane is to treat as common what God has set apart, and Scripture's indictments on the point are addressed most sharply to those whose office was to prevent it. Ezekiel's charge against the priests is comprehensive: “Her priests have violated my law, and have profaned mine holy things: they have put no difference between the holy and profane…and I am profaned among them” (Eze 22:26). The failure named is not open blasphemy but the erasure of a distinction — a refusal to teach the difference — and God says the result is that He Himself is profaned. The commonest way of profaning is by the tongue and the oath: “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God” (Lev 19:12), which is the third commandment applied to daily speech. The New Testament keeps the category and applies it to teaching and to character. Paul tells Timothy to “refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness” (1Ti 4:7) — profane here meaning the merely common dressed up as spiritual. And Hebrews gives the category a face: “Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). Esau is the definition. He was not an atheist; he simply could not see why the holy thing was worth more than a meal, and by the time he wanted the blessing he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.
webster_summary: Common as opposed to holy, and so the treating of sacred things as ordinary; charged against priests who erased the difference between holy and profane, applied to false swearing and to fables taught as godliness, and embodied in Esau, who sold a birthright for a meal.
webster_full: PROFANE, a. 1. Irreverent to any thing sacred; applied to persons. A profane person is one who treats sacred things with contempt or with unbecoming familiarity.
2. Irreverent; proceeding from a contempt of sacred things; as profane words or language.
3. Not sacred; secular; common; relating to secular things; as profane history, in distinction from sacred history.
4. The word is from the Latin pro, before, and fanum, a temple; that which is outside the temple, and therefore not consecrated.
5. PROFANE, v.t. To violate any thing sacred, or treat it with abuse or irreverence. To profane the name of God; to profane the sabbath. Levit. 19; Neh. 13.
scriptures: Ezekiel 22:26

Her priests have violated my law, and have profaned mine holy things: they have put no difference between the holy and profane, neither have they shewed difference between the unclean and the clean, and have hid their eyes from my sabbaths, and I am profaned among them.
Leviticus 19:12
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
1 Timothy 4:7
But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
Hebrews 12:16
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
corruption_summary: The very category of the holy has been dissolved, so that profanity is understood only as coarse language while the far graver profanation Ezekiel names — the erasure of the difference between holy and common — passes without notice.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has narrowed profanity to a matter of vocabulary, and even there it has been domesticated into a question of taste. Scripture's concern is with the treatment of holy things, of which speech is only one instance. The third commandment forbids taking the LORD's name in vain, which covers false swearing, careless invocation, and the whole practice of attaching God's name to what He has not said — a warning that falls heavily on anyone who claims divine authority for his own opinions. Ezekiel's charge cuts deeper still, and it is aimed at ministers: the priests profaned holy things by putting no difference, by declining to teach the distinction, and by hiding their eyes from God's sabbaths. A ministry that blurs what God has separated is doing the thing the prophet condemns, however reverent its tone.

Esau is the pattern the New Testament chooses, and he repays study because nothing in his conduct looks like blasphemy. He came in from the field faint, and he made a rational short-term trade: what profit shall this birthright do to me? The profane man is not necessarily hostile to holy things; he simply prices them at what they will fetch today. That is why profanity in the biblical sense flourishes in a comfortable and religious society, where the birthright can be exchanged for career, respectability, or peace with the age, and the trade will be called realism. Hebrews adds the sober note that Esau afterward found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears — the thing sold could not be bought back at will.
roots_summary: Hebrew chōl is the common as opposed to the holy, and chālal is to pierce, wound, or violate — to profane is to breach what was fenced. Greek bebēlos means what may be trodden by anyone, from bēlos, a threshold.
roots_lines: Hebrew chōl (H2455) — common, profane, ordinary; the opposite of qōdesh, holy, in Eze 22:26 and 44:23.
Hebrew chālal (H2490) — to bore through, to wound, to violate, to profane; the same root gives the word for one slain or pierced.
Hebrew qōdesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing, that which is set apart; the term against which chōl is defined.
Greek bebēlos (G952) — profane, accessible to all, unhallowed; used of profane fables (1Ti 4:7) and of Esau (Heb 12:16).
Greek beblēoō (G953) — to profane, to desecrate; used in Mat 12:5 of the priests who profane the sabbath in the temple and are blameless.
usage: Of the priests' failure to distinguish: they have put no difference between the holy and profane (Eze 22:26).
Of the name and the sabbath: neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God (Lev 19:12); ye profane the sabbath (Neh 13:17-18).
Of persons and teaching: refuse profane and old wives' fables (1Ti 4:7); a profane person, as Esau (Heb 12:16).

etymology: From Old English swēte, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root that also gives Latin suavis and Greek hēdus — the root of English suave and hedonism. Hebrew keeps two quite separate senses under the one English word: māthōq is sweet to the taste, and nīchōach is the sweet savour of sacrifice — a word meaning restful or soothing, so that the smoke of an accepted offering is literally a restful odour to God.
biblical_def: Sweetness in Scripture is the language of delight, and it is applied most persistently to two things: God's word and Christ's sacrifice. Of the word, the psalmist heaps up comparisons and then exceeds them: God's judgments are “More to be desired…than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psa 19:10), and the long psalm makes it personal — “How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psa 119:103). The comparison is deliberate: honey was the sweetest thing an Israelite knew, and the claim is that Scripture surpasses it, which is a claim about affection and not merely about duty. Proverbs extends the same to speech between men: “Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones” (Pro 16:24) — sweetness in the mouth of a friend having a medicinal effect on the body. The second and weightier use is sacrificial. From Noah's offering onward the LORD smells a sweet savour, and the phrase is fulfilled at the cross: Christ “hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” (Eph 5:2). What is soothing and restful to God in that offering is not the suffering as such but the perfect obedience it expressed. Ezekiel and John are also each given a book to eat that is sweet as honey in the mouth and bitter in the belly — a warning that the delightfulness of God's word does not make its message comfortable.
webster_summary: Pleasing to the taste or smell, and so the Bible's standing figure for delight; used above all of God's words, sweeter than honey, and of Christ's self-offering as a sweetsmelling savour restful and acceptable to God.
webster_full: SWEET, a. 1. Agreeable or grateful to the taste; as, sugar and honey are sweet.
2. Pleasing to the smell; fragrant; as sweet spices; the sweet incense of the sanctuary. Exod. 30.
3. Grateful to the ear; melodious; as a sweet voice, sweet melody.
4. Pleasing to the mind; agreeable; as, how sweet are thy words unto my taste. Psalm 119.
5. Sweet savor; in Scripture, the odor of a sacrifice accepted of God; the Hebrew word signifying rest or satisfaction. Gen. 8; Levit. 1; Eph. 5.
scriptures: Psalm 19:10
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
Psalm 119:103
How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
Proverbs 24:13
My son, eat thou honey, because it is good; and the honeycomb, which is sweet to thy taste:
Ephesians 5:2
And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
corruption_summary: Sweetness is taken as the test of truth, so that a doctrine is judged by whether it is pleasant to hear; and against this over-correction sets in, treating any delight in God's word as sentimentality rather than as the response Scripture actually commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah pronounces woe on them that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter, and the inversion is the natural work of a fallen palate. A ministry shaped by what people find sweet will preach the promises without the commands, mercy without judgment, and comfort without repentance — and Jeremiah's verdict on that practice is that they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. Paul foretold the same: the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears. The book eaten in Ezekiel and Revelation is the standing corrective — sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the belly. The word is genuinely delightful and its message is often hard, and any teaching that delivers the first without the second has altered it.

The reaction against sentimentality can, however, go too far, producing a stern piety that treats delight in God as a suspect emotion and duty as the only respectable motive. Scripture will not have this either. The psalms command us to taste and see that the LORD is good, to delight ourselves in Him, to find His words sweeter than honey; the Song of songs is in the canon; and the chief end of man is not merely to glorify God but to enjoy Him for ever. Affection is not the enemy of doctrine but its proper fruit — the Puritans, whose doctrinal rigour is not in question, wrote some of the warmest devotional prose in the language. What is required is that the sweetness follow the truth rather than select it.
roots_summary: Hebrew māthōq is sweet to the taste; nīchōach, from a root meaning to rest, is the sweet savour of an accepted sacrifice. Greek glukus is sweet, and euōdia is a fragrant odour, the New Testament's term for the sacrificial figure.
roots_lines: Hebrew māthōq (H4966) — sweet; used of honey, of the waters of Marah made sweet, and of God's words in Psa 119:103.
Hebrew nīchōach (H5207) — a soothing or restful odour, rendered sweet savour; from nūach, to rest — the offering that satisfies.
Hebrew bōsem (H1314) — spice, sweet odour, balsam; used of the sweet spices for the anointing oil and the incense (Exo 30:23).
Greek glukus (G1099) — sweet; used of the little book sweet as honey in the mouth (Rev 10:9) and of the fountain in Jas 3:11.
Greek euōdia (G2175) — a sweet smell, fragrance; used in Eph 5:2 of Christ's offering and in 2Co 2:15, we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ.
usage: Of God's word: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb (Psa 19:10); how sweet are thy words unto my taste (Psa 119:103).
Of speech between men: pleasant words are as an honeycomb (Pro 16:24); a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver (Pro 25:11).
Of sacrifice: the LORD smelled a sweet savour (Gen 8:21); an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour (Eph 5:2).
